tagline: Old main roads link farmland, canal crossings and working waterfronts.
intro: Chesapeake Country follows winding roads past farms and waterfront towns on Maryland’s Eastern Shore. Visit Maryland presents the drive through the waterways and historic waterfront villages of this tidewater region. The National Scenic Byway portion connects Chesapeake City with Stevensville near the Bay Bridge, with a spur to Eastern Neck Island.

Much of this drive follows MD 213 and MD 18, once main roads and later bypassed by US 50 and US 301. The older corridor passes towns and buildings preserved from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Maryland’s broader Chesapeake Country itinerary extends from Chesapeake City to Crisfield; Visit Maryland gives that longer journey as 419 miles and 12 to 17 driving hours.

Begin at Chesapeake City’s canal and head south on MD 213 through Cecilton, across the Sassafras River and onward through Galena and Kennedyville to Chestertown. At Chestertown, the branch follows MD 20 to Rock Hall and MD 445 to Eastern Neck National Wildlife Refuge. Return to the main route for Centreville, then follow MD 18 through Queenstown and Grasonville onto Kent Island and Stevensville. Stevensville began in 1850 as a steamboat terminal; its historic district contains roughly 100 structures dating to the town’s early days.
notice: At Chesapeake City, modern ships pass Victorian homes and shops along the canal.

moments.title: Chesapeake City
moments.text: The canal divided Chesapeake City; a later bridge changed how travelers reached it. The town adopted its present name in 1839, ten years after the canal was built. A drawbridge joined the two halves until a freighter struck and destroyed it in 1942. Its replacement opened in 1949, high and long enough that cars crossing the canal no longer passed through town. Business declined for decades afterward. The canal remains part of the town’s visible scale: Visit Maryland describes modern ships dwarfing the Victorian homes and shops along its banks.

moments.title: Chestertown
moments.text: Brick mansions and townhouses along the waterfront reflect the wealth of Chestertown’s merchants. Founded in 1706, the town became one of colonial Maryland’s six Royal Ports of Entry. That designation brought a shipping boom to the navigable head of the Chester River. The port declined as Baltimore became the major port for tobacco and wheat; more than fifty Georgian townhouses remain in the district’s collection. The historic residential area concentrates along Water Street, between the business district and the river. It survived the 1910 fire that destroyed the central business district, leaving a distinct eighteenth-century part of town.

moments.title: Rock Hall
moments.text: Rock Hall’s working harbor supports commercial watermen alongside charter fishing and sailing boats. The town once shipped tobacco, seafood and farm products and served colonial passengers. In 1872, the Kent County Railroad proposed linking Massey through Chestertown to a Baltimore ferry connection here for both passengers and freight. But the company went bankrupt in 1877, leaving only a stub from Chestertown to a place called Belair or Parsons and the rest unfinished. Fishing and seafood processing became Rock Hall’s largest industry. Oyster harvesting, crabbing and fishing continue to contribute to its economy.
